DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
**Verdict:** The case for raising prices is sound, but the paper's two key quantitative claims don't hold up against its own data. The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu, not the weakest. And the £42,000 projection leaves out the beef price rise reported in Section 4. Corrected, the price increases mostly absorb the beef cost, and the gain is roughly a third to two-thirds of the figure claimed.

## What holds up

- **The case for a price rise is strong.** Prices haven't changed since September 2024, margin has slipped from 70% to 67%, and the restaurant is the cheapest of its five competitors on all three dishes. The beef rise strengthens the case for the burger and steak increases.
- **The arithmetic in the paper is correct as far as it goes.**
  - The margins in Table 1 match the prices and costs.
  - The volumes sum to 1,050.
  - Weekly gain: £310 + £260 + £240 = £810, and × 52 = £42,120.
  - All three new prices are below the competitor midpoints (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50).
- **Ignoring the beef rise, mains margin would reach about 71%.** I estimate it at about 69–70% now; the exact figure depends on the price of specials, which isn't given.

## Errors

**1. The risotto has the best margin, not the weakest.**

The paper's own figures:

| Dish | Margin % | Margin per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |
| Specials | 64% (lowest) | — |

- Measured either way, the risotto is not the weakest.
- Its sales of 90 a week are the lowest of the named dishes, but they tie with specials.
- It earns about £1,000 a week in gross profit.
- If it is replaced by a special at the specials' average margin of 64% and the same £14 price, gross profit falls by about £200 a week, and the menu's margin falls too.
- It also appears to be the only vegetarian main on the regular menu. That matters for groups, where one vegetarian can determine where the whole party books.

The author calls this decision "clear-cut." The data point the other way: the risotto is a strong performer with modest volume. If any vegetarian dish is to be replaced, the replacement needs to match an 80% margin, not 64%.

**2. The projection leaves out the beef price rise.**

Section 4 says beef rises 12% on 1 April, the same day as the new prices. Section 5.3 counts only the price increases.
- Sirloin is almost all beef, so its food cost rises about £1.25 a plate, or about £150 a week.
- The burger's food cost rises by up to £0.50 a plate, or up to £130 a week, depending on how much of its £4.20 cost is beef.

So £230–280 a week of the £810 goes on higher beef costs. The steak's £2 rise leaves only about 75p of extra margin per plate.

**3. Days of trading.**

Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. The Recommendation says "six trading days a week."

## A question the paper needs to answer: VAT

The paper doesn't say whether margins are calculated on prices including VAT. UK menu prices must include VAT, which is 20% on restaurant food.
- If so, the margins in Table 1 and the £810 are overstated.
- £1 on the menu is about 83p of net revenue, which cuts the weekly gain by about £135 before anything else.
- Restated without VAT, fish and chips earns about 63%, not 69%.
- It also needs to be clear which basis the 70% target and the 67% figure use.

This is open until the author confirms it, and it needs answering before the owners decide.

## Corrected projection

Volumes are assumed unchanged throughout, as the paper assumes.

| Item | Per week |
|---|---|
| Price increases, as in the paper | +£810 |
| Beef cost rise (steak, burger) | −£230 to −£280 |
| Risotto replaced by a special at 64% margin | −£200 (zero if the special matches the risotto) |
| **Net, on the paper's VAT-inclusive basis** | **about +£330 to +£580** |
| Net, if prices are restated without VAT | about +£270 to +£450 |

- Annually, that's about **£14,000–£30,000**, not £42,000.
- Mains margin would end up around **68–69%**, roughly where it is now, rather than rising to 71%.
- In effect, the price rises mostly offset the beef cost increase. That is still worth doing, but it is a different proposal from the one presented.

## Claims that are weaker than presented

- **"Customers are loyal enough to absorb a pound or two."**
  - The 60% figure measures how often guests return, not how they react to prices. Frequent regulars are also the guests most likely to notice increases, as Section 7 itself admits.
  - It counts bookings, not covers, so walk-ins are excluded.
  - Margins are thin enough that volume matters. With the beef rise included, burger and steak volumes only need to fall by about **4–5%** to wipe out the gain, and fish and chips by about **8%**.
- **"We remain the value option."** Today the restaurant is the cheapest on all three dishes. After the change it would be above the cheapest competitor on each, and below the midpoint. "Competitively priced" is accurate; "the value option" is not established.
- **"Every main course" and a "full competitor check."**
  - Specials are pooled in Table 1, not reported dish by dish.
  - The competitor check covers three dishes; curry and risotto aren't priced.
  - These are minor points, but the author's description overstates the evidence.
- **"Weekday lunch is a small share."**
  - This isn't quantified. Friday and Saturday dinner account for just under half of mains, so the other half is spread across the remaining sessions.
  - Weekday lunch could be material, and it's the trade the paper itself calls most price-sensitive.
- **"No visible effect" in 2024.** That refers to bookings in total. It's weak evidence about how many plates of each dish sell at the new prices.

## The monitoring plan will miss what it's meant to catch

- **The baseline is the wrong period.** Plates sold from April to May will be compared with January to February, the quietest months. A normal seasonal rise in spring could hide a fall caused by the price change. Compare with the same weeks of 2025, or with the dishes whose prices aren't changing.
- **It tracks plates per dish, not total gross profit.** Diners switching from steak to curry would show up as falling steak sales and rising curry sales. What matters is whether total mains profit holds.
- **There's no decision rule.** The plan doesn't say what fall in volume would trigger a response, or what that response would be. The break-even falls of about 4–5% and 8% are natural thresholds.

## Suggested revisions

1. Approve the three price increases, and restate the projection net of the beef rise, with the VAT basis made explicit. The expected gain is in the tens of thousands, not £42,000.
2. Withdraw the risotto proposal or reverse its rationale. Keep the risotto unless a vegetarian replacement can be shown to match its margin.
3. Correct "six trading days" to five.
4. Monitor total mains gross profit against the same weeks of 2025. Set thresholds in advance, of about a 5% fall in volume on burger and steak and 8% on fish and chips.
